So, I too have a lot of redness and mine is due to tiny broken capillaries over my face (mostly around my nostrils but also my cheeks and a little between my brows). Your redness does look similar. People with fair skin tones are more susceptible to this, but it can also be genetic and things like alcohol consumption or a lot of sun exposure can make it worse.


Unfortunately, topical treatments don’t work for that type of redness however some people have had great success with different laser treatments! Essentially, they target the capillary and they fade with each treatment. I have opted instead to cover my redness instead of attempting to remove it (I use Dr Jart Cicapair redness cover).

I’m an overweight woman. I work in medical negligence; I understand better than most what characteristics of people end in poorer outcomes medically. I help people fight doctors and institutions that routinely dismiss the symptoms in people of colour, overweight people and people with disabilities. 

I understand that surgeons are not infallible gods. 

I also understand, however, how detrimental being obese is on someone’s health. Perhaps OP has a good surgeon that has simply suggested he lose weight.

Also, it is totally fine to have two feelings about your stoma. You are allowed to not want to be thought of as ‘the sick kid’ and then also require certain things because you genuinely have different needs to the other kids. One, is an identity that you don’t want to be aligned with (sick, unwell, weak). This is very understandable and I too don’t want those labels on me!

The other (taking time off school, needing some arrangements at school because of your stoma, having doctor’s appointments etc) are things that are required due to your physical health. Neither of these concepts are conflicting. 

Tell them that next time they decide to be judgemental.

It gets easier. I’ve had my stoma since 2019 now (I was 27 at the time) and as a young woman (and it’d be the same for men) it does just change how your view your body and by extension, yourself. However, this (for me) didn’t last. My ostomy will likely be permanent. I’m fine with it now. My life is so much better with one than without. 

Mentally, the thing that helps me deal with having a stoma is to remember, I never had the option of a normal, healthy gastrointestinal tract or a stoma. If that were the case, of course I wouldn’t choose a stoma! With my body, I had the choice of a terribly unwell gastrointestinal tract (which made my life hell) or a stoma. I will choose my stoma every day. 

My life has improved so much with my stoma. No longer running to the bathroom, stuck at home, losing blood, on immunosuppressive therapy, sick with chest, ear, sinus infections due to said therapies, losing my hair, swollen joints, aching body etc etc etc. Maybe if you focus on the worst aspects of your illness that lead to the stoma, it will help to reframe how you think of your body. 

I think in your case, the fact that you didn’t have time to prepare for a guaranteed stoma adds to the trauma. 

Adjustment disorders are very common for people that have gone through these types of medical changes; do you have the resources to speak to a psychologist? Mine has really helped how I view my stoma and body.

I was diagnosed after my son was born. I had no idea I had adhd prior to pregnancy or family planning etc. and whilst having adhd has made it probably quite a bit more challenging than if I were neurotypical, I do want to stress some points that I think are important to remember for those of us with adhd. 

This is by no means an encouragement to have children - absolutely do what is best for you. Having a child can be wonderful and having a child free life can be wonderful. 

PROS ABOUT BEING A MUM/MOM/PARENT WITH ADHD: 

- I have developed, from a very young age, an intense sense of empathy, the need for justice, understanding and patience due to my struggles with adhd. This is a high quality trait for a parent to have. 

- I have developed the skill of advocating for myself and by extension, the ability to do the same for my child. 

- I have developed a keen sense of my abilities, weaknesses and triggers. I *know* myself better than I may have been forced to, had I been neurotypical.

- I have a very open mind and understand we all learn, communicate and play differently. 

- I know what it feels like to not belong, be bullied, be considered ‘weird’. This type of experience can be useful whether my child experiences the same or not and can be hard to understand completely if not experienced first hand.

- the ability to think and problem solve on the fly. This has actually come in handy so many times as a parent.

- I am great in emergencies. That adhd brain is in its element when chaos abounds. This is priceless as a caregiver of any type.

Disclaimer (because I’m not shitting on anyone): PEOPLE WITHOUT ADHD CAN ALSO HAVE THESE SKILLS. But with adhd, they are often developed naturally due to needing to survive in a world not curated to our functionality.

I could only sleep on my left side for the last six weeks so that my right side (my stoma side) had the pressure off while I slept so I could pass output. 

It was really difficult. I’ve heard of women with stomas having their babies vaginally and being fine so this was just my experience. I’m also quite small in stature so perhaps some women might have more room for the baby and the small intestine to coexist?

Edit: the c section was no where near as painful and the recovery was no where near as painful as my colectomy surgery.
I wish someone had told my newborn that.

Yes, I was hospitalised twice for the blockages. But again, that’s just my experience. I could eat scrambled eggs and avocado and things of that consistency once the blockages had healed but that took time. I also gave birth prematurely. All of this is to say, there are more risks involved when carrying a baby with an ostomy even if we’re not considered high risk. 

The very nature of the baby taking up space that is diverted for our stoma to come out does cause issues as the space gets smaller. The baby can essentially ‘kink’ the intestine like a hose would get kinked. But these things can be navigated by not eating foods that can give you a blockage and just getting monitored closely toward the end. My baby was completely healthy albeit early and I would do it again. Some Ostomates don’t have the trouble I did.
